argument: Camus argues that the question of whether life is worth living - whether to commit suicide - is the one truly fundamental philosophical question, since every other question is a follow-up to it. Using the myth of Sisyphus as a metaphor for the monotonous, seemingly pointless routine of modern life, he argues that when we ask the universe for meaning we get only silence, producing 'the absurd': the confrontation between our desire for meaning and the world's failure to provide it. Neither physical suicide nor 'philosophical suicide' (escaping into a fabricated other world like religion or ideology) actually resolves that disparity; instead Camus calls us to become 'absurd heroes' who face the absurd honestly and, like Sisyphus, learn to embrace the struggle - even smile at it - without needing it to be meaningful.
keyIdeas: Camus maps the myth of Sisyphus - eternally pushing a boulder up a hill only to watch it roll back down - onto the repetitive, unfulfilling 'up, work, home, TV, bed' cycle of ordinary modern life.

Camus calls the decision of whether to commit suicide 'the one really serious philosophical problem' because every other philosophical question is ultimately a follow-up to whether life, given its apparent meaninglessness, is worth continuing at all.

Asking the universe for meaning and getting only silence reflects a limit of our tools (senses and reason) to establish, with certainty, any cosmic purpose - this is the condition Camus calls the absurd.

Physical suicide fails to solve the absurd because it doesn't fix the mismatch between our desire for meaning and the world's silence, just removing the person from the scene (like fixing a leaky faucet by moving to a different house); 'philosophical suicide' likewise fails by escaping into a fabricated 'other world' - religion being the clearest large-scale example, but also nationalism, ideology, or constant distraction - that supplies a false certainty the real world doesn't provide.

The 'absurd hero' faces the absurd honestly, without resorting to physical or philosophical suicide, and Camus's culminating image of 'Sisyphus smiling' argues that a pointless struggle can still be embraced and even enjoyed, rather than met with resentment.

terms.def: The confrontation between the human need for meaning and reason and the unreasonable silence of the world, born when we ask for cosmic purpose and receive no answer.
Literally ending one's life as an attempted escape from the absurd, which Camus argues fails because it doesn't resolve the underlying mismatch between desire for meaning and the world's silence.
Escaping the absurd by redirecting attention to a fabricated 'other world' that supplies certainty and meaning the real world doesn't provide - religion being Camus's primary example.
Someone who faces the absurd honestly, without resorting to physical or philosophical suicide, which Camus treats as a kind of triumph over the human condition.
The Greek king condemned to eternally push a boulder up a hill only for it to roll back down, used by Camus as a model for embracing meaningless struggle without resentment.
